items.followUp: State two functions of calcium in the human body.

rubric.why: Calcium is a major component of bones and teeth.
rubric.description: Names the role of calcium in bones and teeth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that calcium forms, builds or strengthens bones and teeth.

rubric.why: Calcium also has important roles in blood clotting and muscle activity.
rubric.description: Gives another function of calcium.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either blood clotting or muscle contraction.

modelAnswer: Calcium is needed for the formation and strength of bones and teeth.
It also helps in blood clotting and muscle contraction.

items.followUp: What is a villus, and what does it absorb?

rubric.why: A lacteal is the lymphatic vessel found in an intestinal villus.
rubric.description: Identifies the location and nature of a lacteal.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as a lymph vessel in a villus.

rubric.why: Lacteals take up the products of fat digestion.
rubric.description: States what a lacteal absorbs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying absorbed fats or their digestion products.

modelAnswer: A lacteal is a lymph vessel present in a villus of the small intestine.
It absorbs the products of fat digestion, mainly fatty acids and glycerol.

items.followUp: Name two factors that may increase the risk of leukaemia.

rubric.why: Exposure to radiation or certain harmful chemicals is associated with leukaemia.
rubric.description: Names an environmental risk factor.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for radiation or harmful/carcinogenic chemicals.

rubric.why: Genetic changes and some viral infections may also be involved; the precise cause is not always known.
rubric.description: Names another possible cause or notes the role of genetic changes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for genetic changes, mutation or a viral cause.

modelAnswer: Leukaemia involves abnormal, uncontrolled production of white blood cells; its exact cause is not always known.
Possible causes or risk factors include exposure to radiation and certain harmful chemicals.
Genetic changes and some viral infections may also be involved.

items.followUp: Where are the mitral and tricuspid valves located, and how many cusps does each have?

rubric.why: The bicuspid valve is between the left atrium and left ventricle.
rubric.description: Gives the location of the bicuspid valve.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for placing it between the left atrium and ventricle.

rubric.why: The bicuspid valve has two cusps.
rubric.description: States the number of cusps of the bicuspid valve.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two cusps or flaps.

rubric.why: The tricuspid valve is on the right side of the heart.
rubric.description: Gives the location of the tricuspid valve.
rubric.how: This comparison point is assessed together with the cusp distinction; award marks within the 2-mark total.

rubric.why: The tricuspid valve has three cusps.
rubric.description: States the number of cusps of the tricuspid valve.
rubric.how: This comparison point is assessed together with the cusp distinction; award marks within the 2-mark total.

modelAnswer: The bicuspid (mitral) valve lies between the left atrium and left ventricle and has two cusps.
The tricuspid valve lies between the right atrium and right ventricle and has three cusps.

items.followUp: Define transpiration and name two environmental factors that affect its rate.

rubric.why: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, especially the leaves.
rubric.description: Defines transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing loss of water vapour from aerial plant parts.

rubric.why: Higher temperature or light intensity generally increases transpiration.
rubric.description: Names temperature or light as a factor and gives its general effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct factor-effect relationship.

rubric.why: High humidity slows transpiration, while moving air commonly increases it.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of humidity or wind.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect of humidity or wind.

rubric.why: A shortage of water in the soil reduces water uptake and therefore lowers transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of water availability in the soil.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for naming soil water availability and 1 for correctly relating reduced supply to a lower rate.

modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
Higher temperature and greater light intensity generally increase the rate of transpiration.
High humidity lowers the rate because the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air is reduced.
Wind generally increases the rate by carrying water vapour away from the leaf surface.
A shortage of water in the soil reduces water uptake and lowers the rate of transpiration.

items.followUp: Describe two causes of deforestation and two effects it has on the environment.

rubric.why: Forests are cleared for farming, timber, fuel and expanding settlements.
rubric.description: Names human activities that cause deforestation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one or more valid causes.

rubric.why: Removing trees can increase soil erosion and flooding and destroy habitats.
rubric.description: Gives an environmental effect of deforestation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one or more valid effects such as erosion, flooding or habitat loss.

rubric.why: Fewer trees means less carbon dioxide is removed from the atmosphere, contributing to climate change.
rubric.description: Explains an atmospheric or climate effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking deforestation with increased carbon dioxide, global warming or climate change.

rubric.why: Deforestation can disrupt the water cycle and harm ecosystems and species.
rubric.description: Gives another environmental consequence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for another valid effect, such as reduced rainfall, desertification or species loss.

modelAnswer: Causes include clearing forests for agriculture and cutting trees for timber or fuel; forests are also cleared for settlements and roads.
Deforestation removes habitats and reduces biodiversity.
It exposes soil to erosion and can increase flooding.
It also reduces carbon dioxide uptake, contributing to global warming and climate change, and may disrupt the water cycle.

items.followUp: Describe how water is split during the light reactions of photosynthesis and state the products formed.

rubric.why: The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes, where chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.description: Names the site or the role of chlorophyll and light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the thylakoid/grana location or for chlorophyll absorbing light.

rubric.why: Light energy drives the splitting of water, or photolysis.
rubric.description: Describes photolysis of water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light splits water.

rubric.why: Oxygen is released as a product of water splitting.
rubric.description: Identifies oxygen as a product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oxygen being produced or released.

rubric.why: The light reactions produce ATP and reduced NADP for use in the subsequent reactions.
rubric.description: Names the energy and reducing products.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for ATP and reduced NADP (NADPH/NADPH2).

rubric.why: The diagram should show the light-driven electron pathway and the main products of the reactions.
rubric.description: Includes a correctly labelled schematic of the light-reaction pathway.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear schematic showing the light reactions, water splitting and formation of ATP/NADPH, with key labels.

modelAnswer: The light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast, where chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
Light energy drives photolysis: water is split into hydrogen ions, electrons and oxygen; oxygen is released.
Light-excited electrons pass through electron carriers, and their energy is used to form ATP.
Electrons reaching photosystem I help reduce NADP to NADPH (reduced NADP).
The ATP and NADPH formed are used in the subsequent reactions of photosynthesis.
Diagram (schematic): H₂O → O₂ + H⁺ + e⁻; light → Photosystem II → electron transport chain → Photosystem I → NADP⁺ → NADPH.
Label ATP formation from the electron transport chain, and show light entering both photosystems.

items.followUp: Name the main parts of a chloroplast and state its function.

rubric.why: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells.
rubric.description: Defines plastids as membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition identifying plastids as organelles bounded by a membrane.

rubric.why: Plastids occur in plant cells.
rubric.description: States where plastids are found.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying plant cells.

rubric.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Identifies chlorophyll and/or the chloroplast's function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chlorophyll or photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The chloroplast contains grana made of thylakoids, surrounded by stroma.
rubric.description: Names key internal chloroplast structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming grana/thylakoids and stroma.

modelAnswer: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in the cells of plants.
Chloroplasts are green plastids containing the pigment chlorophyll.
They are the site of photosynthesis.
A chloroplast is bounded by a double membrane and contains fluid stroma and grana made of stacks of thylakoids.
